catalog_quote: The two important structural elements are “tone” and “doubling”; and the important consequence concerns syllabic and/or homorganic nasals. Tone is here defined as the distribution of vocal tension over the syllable. Since its domain is fixed, i.e. the syllable, and since this domain is necessarily greater than a single segment in at least some cases, then tone is considered as an element of the structure rather than of any segment. ... Therefore, this part of the syllable, which is the syllable peak in Hockett’s terms, is regarded as the tone-bearing segment. Every nucleus must bear a tone, of which there are four contrastive possibilities in the Ekoid Bantu Languages. These possibilities ... 1. High: a level of relatively greatest vocal tension; 2. new_statements.rule_in_words: Ndoe (Crabb's languages A Ekparabong and B Balep, two of the fourteen 'Ekoid Bantu Languages' the phonology covers) is described as a syllable-tone language: every syllable nucleus carries one of four contrastive tones (H, L, F, R; a fifth Mid mainly in other Ekoid lects). The phonology has no stress or accent section and the word 'stress' does not occur in the volume; on p.12 Crabb explicitly rejects Bystrom's (1954) amateur claim that 'Ekparabong is not like Efik a tone language'. Blench's open ms (p.6, on file) concurs for Ekoid as a whole: 'High, Low, Rising, Falling and Downstep tones', nothing on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The only dissent on prosodic type is Bystrom 1954 (non-linguist) who denied Ekparabong is tonal; Crabb (p.12) dismisses this and his own Ekparabong/Balep data are fully tone-marked. Mid tone is said to be needed 'especially in languages N, O, P, T, and U' (Nde, Nselle, Nta, Nnam, Ekajuk), i.e. not specifically for A/B.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone domain = the syllable (each nucleus). Statement is Ekoid-wide (14 lects incl. A Ekparabong and B Balep), based on elicited citation forms from one informant per lect (A: W.E. Ojong of Akparabong; B: J.E. Ndoma of Balep, Ikom Division). No word- or phrase-level stress statement exists anywhere in the accessible record.
new_statements.identity_note: Crabb 1965 treats Ndoe as two lects: language A = Ekparabong (Glottolog dialect ekpa1238; informant from Akparabong, Ikom Division) and language B = Balep (bale1253; 'forms one speech community with Opu'). The quoted tone statement is scoped to all fourteen 'Ekoid Bantu Languages' A-U, not to Ndoe alone; the Mid tone is flagged mainly for N, O, P, T, U (Nde, Nselle, Nta, Nnam, Ekajuk), so A/B are described with the four-tone H/L/F/R system. Blench's corroborating statement is Ekoid(-Mbe)-wide.
